newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Ever First to buy control of Liang Shing.
newsitem.headline: Ever First to buy control of Liang Shing.

text.p: Footwear and property investment firm Liang Shing (Holdings) Ltd said it would issue 250 million new shares or 42.7 percent of its enlarged share capital to Ever First Investments Ltd at HK$0.138 per share.

Ever First had also agreed to buy a total 154.36 million existing shares, representing 26.3 percent of Liang Shing's enlarged share capital, and 30.8 million warrants or 55 percent of its issued warrants from major shareholders Pherson Management Inc and the Ma family at HK$0.138 per share and HK$0.01 for every 10,000 warrants.
Ever First would then make a general offer for all outstanding shares and warrants of Liang Shing at the same price per share and warrant, the statement said.
Trading in Liang Shing shares which had been suspended since March 3, resumed on Thursday. Its shares rose HK$0.055 or 19.64 percent to HK$0.335 in early trade.

Ever First is 55 percent owned by a third-party First Place Ltd and 45 percent by Gleeson Trading Ltd, a company 40 percent owned by Liang Shing's chairman Chang Tsung Yuan and 60 percent by the Ma family of the late Liang Shing chairman David Ma.

"The purpose of the subscription agreement is to raise additional funds and increase the level of equity capital of Liang Shing to help retain the confidence of the financiers and creditors of Liang Shing," the company said in a statement.
The net proceeds of about HK$34.5 million from the new issue will be used for working capital, Liang Shing said.

The statement said Ever First would buy from Chang-controlled Pherson its 43.96 million existing shares and 8.79 million warrants in Liang Shing, and 110.04 million shares and 22.01 million warrants from Ma family.
"Ever First may consider diversifying and strengthening the group's income and capital bases by acquisition of new assets or businesses," the statement said.
Meanwhile, Liang Shing said it expected to record a substantial loss for the year ended in December 1996 due to the depressed export market for shoes and the death of David Ma in August 1996.

The company said it had encountered difficult operating conditions since the second half of 1996 and provisions against investments in manufacturing facilities, stocks and receivables were likety to be made.
